subjects.label: Coding
subjects.audience: software engineers from junior to staff, global English-speaking
subjects.style: mechanism-first engineering teaching; use runnable code only where code itself is the lesson (syntax, an algorithm, an API, a bug) — for conceptual/theory topics show the mechanism visually instead of a code listing

modules.label: Frontend
modules.style: the browser is the machine: teach what actually happens at runtime (parse, render, paint, bundle, hydrate) with real DevTools evidence and numbers; trace every framework abstraction down to the DOM/network reality beneath it

submodules.label: JavaScript
submodules.style: The language runtime itself — event loop, closures, prototypes, coercion, async — never React or types. Great episodes trace code through the call stack and task queues. Credibility comes from console-provable snippets, V8 behaviors, and spec terms like TDZ and microtask.

submodules.label: CSS & Browser
submodules.style: How the browser turns CSS into pixels: cascade, specificity, flexbox/grid, layout-paint-composite, Core Web Vitals. JS appears only to prove rendering claims. Great episodes lean on DevTools evidence. Credibility: the 16.7ms frame budget, which properties trigger layout, real LCP and CLS numbers.

submodules.label: TypeScript
submodules.style: The type system, never runtime behavior: narrowing, generics, structural typing, tsconfig strictness. Great episodes show the compiler catching a bug JavaScript would ship. Credibility: exact error codes (TS2345), what each strict flag changes, utility types like Partial and Pick, version-specific features.

submodules.label: React
submodules.style: React's client rendering model — re-renders, reconciliation, hooks rules, state, memo. Server components and routing belong to Next.js. Great episodes prove WHY a component re-rendered. Credibility: React DevTools profiler evidence, useEffect dependency traps, StrictMode double-invoke, exact hook signatures.

submodules.label: Next.js
submodules.style: The framework layer above React: App Router, server components, SSR/SSG/ISR, caching, hydration. Great episodes pin down where code runs — server or client — and prove it. Credibility: file conventions (page.tsx, 'use client'), fetch cache options, build output, App-vs-Pages Router gotchas.

submodules.label: Web Performance
submodules.style: making pages feel instant — Core Web Vitals, the critical rendering path, lazy loading, code splitting, image strategy, caching. Great episodes show a Lighthouse score moving and attribute every millisecond.

submodules.label: Web Security & Accessibility
submodules.style: the frontend's duty of care — XSS, CSRF, CORS, CSP, clickjacking, plus semantic HTML, ARIA, keyboard and screen-reader accessibility. Great episodes demo one real exploit (safely) or one real assistive-tech flow.

exemplars.short:
TITLE: Promises always beat setTimeout: the microtask queue
HOOK: setTimeout(fn, 0) does not run in zero milliseconds — and a one-line Promise will jump the queue ahead of it every single time.
ARC: 1) Run setTimeout(() => log('timeout'), 0) then Promise.resolve().then(() => log('promise')) — the promise logs first, every time, in every browser. 2) After each task the event loop drains the ENTIRE microtask queue before touching the next macrotask; setTimeout callbacks are macrotasks, and per the HTML spec deeply nested timeouts clamp to a 4ms minimum anyway. 3) That is also why an endless chain of promises can starve rendering — microtasks never yield to paint.
PAYOFF: setTimeout's delay is a minimum wait, not a schedule — which queue you are in matters more than the number you pass.
QUESTION: Is there ever a legitimate reason to use setTimeout(0) instead of queueMicrotask? Defend one.
exemplars.long:
TITLE: 16 milliseconds: the browser's frame deadline
HOOK: Your screen repaints 60 times a second, which gives your JavaScript about 16.7 milliseconds per frame — miss the deadline and users call your app janky.
ARC: 1) HTML becomes the DOM, CSS becomes the CSSOM, and they merge into the render tree — watch it as Parse HTML and Recalculate Style in the DevTools Performance panel. 2) Layout computes geometry; reading offsetHeight right after writing styles forces a synchronous reflow, and doing it in a loop is classic layout thrashing. 3) Paint rasterizes layers and the compositor stitches them on the GPU — transform and opacity skip layout AND paint, which is why they animate smoothly. 4) Chrome flags any task over 50ms as a Long Task; batch your DOM reads and writes, or move work into requestAnimationFrame. 5) Re-profile: the flame chart shows the purple layout blocks gone.
PAYOFF: The fastest CSS property is the one that never triggers layout — animate transform and opacity and the compositor does the work off the main thread.
QUESTION: Is will-change a legitimate optimization or a footgun that leaks GPU memory in your codebase?

modules.label: Backend
modules.style: follow one real request end to end — routing, middleware, serialization, the process model; real framework code, typical latency numbers, and the production failure mode that bites

submodules.label: Python
submodules.style: Python the language and CPython the runtime: object model, GIL, asyncio, decorators, typing — no web frameworks here. Great episodes reveal what the interpreter actually does. Credibility: dis and sys demos, GIL behavior under threads, version facts (3.12 speedups, 3.13's experimental free-threaded build).

submodules.label: API Design
submodules.style: Language-agnostic contract design: REST semantics, status codes, versioning, pagination, idempotency, auth patterns, webhooks. Framework internals live in the framework lanes. Great episodes autopsy real public APIs. Credibility: Stripe and GitHub examples, correct 409-vs-422 calls, Idempotency-Key headers, cursor-vs-offset trade-offs.

submodules.label: FastAPI
submodules.style: FastAPI and its stack — Pydantic, Starlette, uvicorn, dependency injection, async endpoints. Language internals go to Python; HTTP semantics to API Design. Great episodes follow one request through the framework. Credibility: def-vs-async-def threadpool behavior, Pydantic v2's Rust core, uvicorn worker flags.

submodules.label: Backend Production
submodules.style: shipping Python services for real — Docker images, health checks, graceful shutdown, logging/metrics/tracing, CI/CD, pooling, queues, load testing. Great episodes trace one deploy from git push to serving traffic and name the failure it prevents.

exemplars.short:
TITLE: One million goroutines: Go's 2KB trick
HOOK: Spawning a million OS threads will take down a Linux box — Go programs spawn a million goroutines and barely notice. The difference is one number: 2 kilobytes.
ARC: 1) A pthread on Linux defaults to an 8MB stack — ulimit -s prints 8192 — so a million threads means terabytes of virtual memory plus a brutal kernel context-switch tax. 2) A goroutine starts at 2KB and grows its stack on demand, while the runtime multiplexes goroutines onto a small pool of OS threads sized by GOMAXPROCS, which defaults to your CPU count. 3) Goroutines blocked on channels or network I/O get parked off-thread by the netpoller, so 10,000 idle connections cost megabytes, not gigabytes.
PAYOFF: Cheap concurrency is really a memory-layout decision — tiny growable stacks are what make go func() an unremarkable thing to type.
QUESTION: Do you still bother with worker pools in Go, or just spawn a goroutine per job?
exemplars.long:
TITLE: One request through FastAPI: the whole journey
HOOK: Changing def to async def on a FastAPI endpoint changes which thread your code runs on — and under load, that one keyword decides whether requests pile up or flow.
ARC: 1) The kernel accepts the TCP connection and uvicorn — an ASGI server built on uvloop and httptools — parses HTTP and hands FastAPI a scope dict, not a request object. 2) Starlette matches the route, middleware wraps the call like an onion, and your Depends() graph resolves before the handler runs. 3) Pydantic v2 validates the body in compiled Rust (pydantic-core) — several times faster than the pure-Python v1. 4) async def handlers run on the event loop; plain def handlers are shipped to a threadpool that AnyIO caps at 40 threads by default — and one time.sleep() inside async def stalls every request in the process. 5) Your returned dict is serialized to a JSONResponse and written back through the same ASGI send channel.
PAYOFF: FastAPI is fast because the slow parts — parsing, validation — were pushed down to C and Rust; the only thing that ruins it is you blocking the loop.
QUESTION: def or async def for a handler calling a sync database driver — what do you ship, and why?

modules.label: DSA & Interviews
modules.style: interview-first: open on the problem class that filters candidates, show the naive way dying (count the operations), then the insight, then the reusable pattern; complexity always stated AND shown

submodules.label: Big-O & Complexity
submodules.style: Complexity analysis itself: reading growth rates off code, amortized costs, space-time trades — no single algorithm owns this lane. Great episodes count real operations, then time real runs to match the math. Credibility: measured timings at n = 10³ versus 10⁶, amortized append analysis, log₂ arithmetic.

submodules.label: Arrays & Strings
submodules.style: Linear-structure interview patterns: two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums, hashing over arrays and strings. Trees and graphs live next door. Great episodes show the naive O(n²) dying before the pattern rescues it. Credibility: named LeetCode problems, operation counts at n = 10⁵, runnable code.

submodules.label: Hashing & Hash Maps
submodules.style: hash maps as the interview workhorse — hash functions, collisions, load factor, and the classic patterns (frequency count, two-sum, seen-sets). Great episodes show WHY O(1) lookup isn't magic and when it degrades.

submodules.label: Linked Lists
submodules.style: pointers you can draw — traversal, reversal, fast/slow runners, cycle detection, dummy heads. Great episodes animate the pointer surgery step by step and name the off-by-one traps.

submodules.label: Stacks & Queues
submodules.style: LIFO/FIFO as thinking tools — parentheses matching, monotonic stacks, queue-via-stacks, deques and sliding windows. Great episodes show the moment a problem 'becomes' a stack problem.

submodules.label: Sorting & Searching
submodules.style: Ordering and lookup: binary search and its variants, quicksort/mergesort/heapsort mechanics, when the built-in sort is the right answer. Great episodes expose off-by-one traps and pivot disasters. Credibility: Timsort inside Python and Java, the O(n log n) comparison-sort lower bound, mid-computation overflow lore.

submodules.label: Heaps & Priority Queues
submodules.style: the structure behind 'top-K' — heap property, sift up/down, heapify in O(n), K-way merge, two-heap median. Great episodes contrast heap vs sorting and show real heapq/PriorityQueue code.

submodules.label: Trees & Graphs
submodules.style: Hierarchies and networks: BFS/DFS, binary search trees, topological sort, union-find. Great episodes pick the traversal from what the problem is really asking. Credibility: recursion versus explicit stack, adjacency list versus matrix costs, canonical problems like Number of Islands and Course Schedule.

submodules.label: Recursion & Backtracking
submodules.style: trust the recursion — base cases, call trees, then backtracking's choose/explore/un-choose loop for permutations, subsets, N-queens, Sudoku. Great episodes draw the decision tree and prune it on screen.

submodules.label: Greedy Algorithms
submodules.style: when local best is global best — exchange arguments, interval scheduling, jump game, Huffman. Great episodes also show a greedy FAILURE (coin change 1/3/4) so viewers learn when greedy is wrong.

submodules.label: Bit Manipulation & Math
submodules.style: bits and number theory interviewers love — XOR tricks, masks, power-of-two checks, GCD, modular arithmetic, fast exponentiation. Great episodes make one bit trick feel like a magic reveal, then demystify it.

submodules.label: Dynamic Programming
submodules.style: Overlapping-subproblem optimization: memoization, tabulation, state design, space compression. No repeated subproblem means it is not this lane. Great episodes derive the recurrence live rather than announcing it. Credibility: call-count math (naive fib(50) is about 40 billion calls), named problems — edit distance, knapsack, LIS.

exemplars.short:
TITLE: Two Sum in one pass: the hash map insight
HOOK: Two Sum is LeetCode problem number one, and the answer that feels obvious is exactly the one that gets you rejected.
ARC: 1) Nested loops check every pair — n(n-1)/2 comparisons, so at n = 100,000 that is around five billion operations and a guaranteed time-limit-exceeded. 2) One pass with a hash map flips the question: for each x, have I already seen target minus x? Lookup is O(1) average, the whole scan O(n) time and O(n) space. 3) The reusable pattern is trading memory for a question — 'have I seen this before?' is the cheapest question in computing.
PAYOFF: Interviews rarely test the data structure — they test whether you notice the inner loop is asking a question a hash map answers in constant time.
QUESTION: If the array came pre-sorted, do you write the hash map or two pointers — and which does your interviewer secretly want?
exemplars.long:
TITLE: 40 billion calls: fixing recursive Fibonacci
HOOK: fib(50) written the textbook way makes over 40 billion function calls to compute one number your phone's calculator returns instantly. Every dynamic programming problem is this bug in disguise.
ARC: 1) Trace the call tree: fib(48) is computed twice, fib(47) three times — total calls come to 2·fib(51)−1, roughly 40.7 billion, growing at O(φⁿ). 2) Memoization caches answers by argument, collapsing the tree to 51 unique calls — in Python, @functools.lru_cache does it in one line. 3) Tabulation flips it bottom-up into an array filled left to right — no recursion, so CPython's default 1000-frame recursion limit stops mattering. 4) Only two previous values are ever read, so the O(n) array shrinks to two variables: O(1) space. 5) The same recipe — define the state, find the transition, cache overlapping subproblems — cracks coin change, edit distance, and house robber.
PAYOFF: DP is not a topic, it is an observation: when the call tree repeats itself, cache it — everything after that is bookkeeping.
QUESTION: Memoization or tabulation as your interview default — and which one has actually bitten you?

modules.label: Database
modules.style: real tables on screen, not prose about tables: show the rows, the query, the plan; teach what the engine does — indexes, locks, joins — through one worked dataset per video

submodules.label: SQL
submodules.style: The query language, engine-agnostic: joins, GROUP BY, subqueries, window functions, NULL semantics, CTEs. Engine internals belong to PostgreSQL; speed tuning to Indexing. Great episodes run every query against a visible dataset. Credibility: logical clause order (FROM before SELECT), three-valued-logic traps, exact syntax.

submodules.label: PostgreSQL
submodules.style: Postgres the engine: MVCC, VACUUM, WAL, transactions and isolation levels, psql tooling, extensions. Portable SQL stays in the SQL lane. Great episodes prove engine behavior with system catalogs. Credibility: pg_stat views, EXPLAIN output, defaults like port 5432, version facts (MERGE landed in 15).

submodules.label: Indexing & Performance
submodules.style: Making queries fast on any engine: B-trees, query plans, composite and covering indexes, N+1 queries, lock contention. Great episodes measure before and after, reading the plan aloud. Credibility: EXPLAIN ANALYZE timings, 8KB page math, the leading-column rule, the write tax every index adds.

submodules.label: Transactions & Concurrency
submodules.style: the ACID heart of databases — isolation levels and their anomalies (dirty/non-repeatable/phantom, write skew), MVCC vs locking, deadlocks, idempotency, sagas/2PC. Great episodes reproduce an anomaly with two terminal sessions.

submodules.label: NoSQL
submodules.style: The category and its trade-offs: key-value, document, wide-column, and graph models, CAP, denormalization, and when relational still wins. Specific engines get their own lanes. Great episodes match data model to access pattern. Credibility: named systems (DynamoDB, Redis), real consistency menus, honest 'don't use NoSQL here' calls.

submodules.label: MongoDB
submodules.style: MongoDB specifics: documents and BSON, aggregation pipelines, indexes, replica sets, schema design without joins. Category-level NoSQL arguments go next door. Great episodes design the schema around the query pattern. Credibility: real aggregation stages ($match, $group, $lookup), the 16MB document limit, writeConcern semantics.

submodules.label: Cassandra
submodules.style: Cassandra's wide-column world: partition keys, LSM-tree storage, tunable consistency, query-first data modeling. Great episodes explain why writes are cheap and ad-hoc queries are forbidden. Credibility: CQL-versus-SQL differences, quorum math at RF=3, the memtable-SSTable-compaction flow, tombstone gotchas.

exemplars.short:
TITLE: The rows SQL silently hides: NULL logic
HOOK: WHERE status != 'cancelled' looks airtight — and it quietly throws away every row where status is NULL. No error, no warning, just missing data.
ARC: 1) SQL comparisons return TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE — run SELECT NULL = NULL and the answer is NULL, not true. 2) NOT IN is crueler: one NULL inside the list makes the whole query return zero rows. 3) The fixes are explicit: IS DISTINCT FROM in Postgres, COALESCE before comparing, and knowing COUNT(col) skips NULLs while COUNT(*) doesn't — the classic dashboard mismatch.
PAYOFF: NULL isn't a value, it's a claim of ignorance — and SQL refuses to say TRUE about anything it doesn't know.
QUESTION: Should new schemas ban NULLs with NOT NULL everywhere — or where do you deliberately allow them?
exemplars.long:
TITLE: Reading the query plan: one index, ten million rows
HOOK: EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a ten-million-row table prints 'Seq Scan' — Postgres just admitted it read every single row to find your one user.
ARC: 1) Build the table with generate_series; WHERE email = ... without an index sequentially scans every 8KB heap page — hundreds of milliseconds even when cached. 2) CREATE INDEX ON users(email) builds a B-tree; each 8KB page holds hundreds of keys, so the tree stays 3-4 levels tall at tens of millions of rows — a handful of page reads instead of millions. 3) Rerun EXPLAIN ANALYZE: Index Scan, under a millisecond — but LIKE '%gmail.com' still seq-scans, because B-trees only match left-anchored prefixes. 4) A composite index on (a, b) is useless for filters on b alone — the leading-column rule makes column order a design decision. 5) The bill: every INSERT and UPDATE now writes index pages too, and pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan exposes the indexes nobody reads.
PAYOFF: An index is a bet — you pay on every write to win on specific reads, and the query plan tells you whether the bet is paying off.
QUESTION: How many indexes on one hot table before you call it a smell — five, ten, more?

modules.label: DevOps
modules.style: from laptop to production: teach the actual files and commands (Dockerfile, YAML, IAM policy) line by line and what each buys; one real deploy/ops war story where it fits

submodules.label: Linux & Shell
submodules.style: The OS surface engineers actually touch: filesystem and permissions, processes and signals, pipes, systemd, bash scripting, debugging tools. Great episodes make one command's real behavior click. Credibility: exact flags (chmod 755, kill -15 versus -9), /proc spelunking, strace output, exit codes.

submodules.label: Docker
submodules.style: Containers and images on one machine: Dockerfile mechanics, layers and caching, namespaces and cgroups underneath, Compose, registries. Multi-machine orchestration is Kubernetes' lane. Great episodes shrink an image or bust a caching myth live. Credibility: exact instructions, image-size numbers, multi-stage builds, docker inspect evidence.

submodules.label: CI/CD
submodules.style: Pipelines from push to production: GitHub Actions and GitLab CI syntax, build-test-deploy stages, artifacts, secrets, blue-green and canary deploys, rollbacks. Great episodes debug a real failing pipeline or ship a safe deploy. Credibility: actual YAML, cache-hit savings, deployment gates, honest pipeline-duration numbers.

submodules.label: AWS
submodules.style: AWS services and their sharp edges: IAM, EC2, S3, Lambda, VPC, and the cost traps between them. GCP-first content lives next door. Great episodes build one small real thing and show the bill. Credibility: hard limits (Lambda's 15-minute timeout), IAM policy JSON, S3 storage classes, egress pricing.

submodules.label: GCP
submodules.style: Google Cloud's take: Cloud Run, GKE, BigQuery, IAM differences, the project and billing model. AWS comparisons welcome; AWS-first content belongs next door. Great episodes highlight where GCP's model genuinely differs. Credibility: gcloud commands, BigQuery's per-TB-scanned pricing, Cloud Run scale-to-zero and cold starts.

submodules.label: Kubernetes
submodules.style: Orchestration: pods, Deployments, Services, the control loop, scheduling, probes, autoscaling. Single-machine container mechanics stay with Docker. Great episodes trace desired state to running container through named components. Credibility: kubectl commands, YAML fields (livenessProbe, resources.limits), kubelet/etcd/kube-scheduler roles, CrashLoopBackOff behavior.

submodules.label: Terraform & IaC
submodules.style: Infrastructure as code: HCL, providers, the plan/apply lifecycle, state files, modules, drift. Console click-ops belongs in the cloud lanes. Great episodes read the plan diff and show what state actually stores. Credibility: terraform plan output, state locking with S3 plus DynamoDB, count-versus-for_each gotchas.

submodules.label: Observability & SRE
submodules.style: seeing production — structured logs, metrics, traces, Prometheus/Grafana, SLI/SLO/error budgets, alerting that doesn't page at 3am for nothing, incident response. Great episodes debug one simulated outage end to end.

exemplars.short:
TITLE: Swap two Dockerfile lines: instant rebuilds
HOOK: Every code change forcing a full npm install isn't Docker being slow — it's your COPY line sitting one instruction too early.
ARC: 1) Each Dockerfile instruction becomes a cached layer, and a change invalidates that layer plus everything after it — so COPY . . before RUN npm install reinstalls node_modules on every edit. 2) Copy package.json and package-lock.json first, install, THEN copy the source: the dependency layer stays cached until the lockfile changes, and rebuilds drop from minutes to seconds. 3) The same trick is universal — requirements.txt before app code in Python, go.mod before source in Go.
PAYOFF: Docker's cache is deliberately dumb — it checksums per instruction — so you order instructions from least- to most-frequently changed.
QUESTION: Multi-stage builds or --mount=type=cache — which one has saved you more real minutes?
exemplars.long:
TITLE: kubectl apply to running pod: the control loop
HOOK: kubectl apply returns in half a second, but nothing you typed starts a container — five separate programs negotiate that behind your back.
ARC: 1) kubectl POSTs your YAML to the API server on port 6443; after authentication and admission webhooks, the Deployment is just a record persisted to etcd, a Raft-replicated key-value store — no container exists yet. 2) The deployment controller sees desired ≠ actual and creates a ReplicaSet, which creates Pod objects — still only etcd entries with no node assigned. 3) kube-scheduler watches for unscheduled pods, filters nodes on resources, taints, and affinity, scores the survivors, and writes one node name onto the pod. 4) That node's kubelet notices the binding and drives containerd through CRI to pull the image and start containers; repeated crashes back off exponentially — CrashLoopBackOff caps at five minutes. 5) The loop never stops: delete the pod and the ReplicaSet controller recreates it within seconds.
PAYOFF: Kubernetes isn't a deployment tool, it's a reconciliation engine — you edit a database record and controllers fight reality until it matches.
QUESTION: Below what scale is Kubernetes overkill — five services, twenty, fifty?

modules.label: System Design
modules.style: numbers drive decisions: QPS, latency budgets, storage math; every pattern anchored in a named company's real architecture and the trade-off they accepted

submodules.label: The Interview Toolkit
submodules.style: the system design interview as a skill — requirements, back-of-envelope estimation, API and data-model choices, deep dives, trade-off talk, 45-minute pacing. Great episodes run a real mock segment and grade it out loud.

submodules.label: Design Patterns
submodules.style: The building blocks on the request path: client-server, load balancers (L4 versus L7), API gateways, monolith versus microservices, stateless design. Capacity math belongs to Scaling. Great episodes place each block on a traced request. Credibility: nginx/HAProxy/Envoy specifics, health-check configs, real request-path diagrams.

submodules.label: Caching & Queues
submodules.style: The two great decouplers: cache placement and invalidation, TTLs, stampedes, plus queues, backpressure, and delivery guarantees. Engine internals belong to Key Technologies. Great episodes pick the strategy from the failure mode. Credibility: cache-aside versus write-through trade-offs, at-least-once honesty, hit-rate math.

submodules.label: Scaling & Sharding
submodules.style: Growing past one machine: vertical versus horizontal, partitioning strategies, consistent hashing, hot keys, capacity math. Cache tactics live in Caching & Queues. Great episodes do the arithmetic on screen — QPS, storage, growth. Credibility: hash-ring mechanics, Instagram's sharded-Postgres ID scheme, back-of-envelope numbers that check out.

submodules.label: Replication & Consistency
submodules.style: Keeping copies agreeing: leader-follower setups, quorums, replication lag, CAP in practice, isolation levels. Consensus algorithms and clocks go to Distributed Systems. Great episodes show a stale read happening, then fix it. Credibility: R+W>N arithmetic, read-your-writes techniques, Postgres streaming replication versus DynamoDB's consistency menu.

submodules.label: Distributed Systems
submodules.style: The hard theory made usable: consensus (Raft, Paxos), clocks and ordering, failure detection, idempotency, the exactly-once myth. Replication topologies sit next door. Great episodes prove why the naive distributed version breaks. Credibility: Raft terms and elections, Lamport clocks, Two Generals, Jepsen findings.

submodules.label: Real-World Architectures
submodules.style: Whole named systems end to end: how Netflix, Uber, WhatsApp, or Discord actually built it, every component chosen for a stated reason. Isolated patterns belong in the other lanes. Great episodes cite engineering blogs and talks. Credibility: published numbers only — Discord's Cassandra-to-ScyllaDB migration, WhatsApp's famously tiny team.

exemplars.short:
TITLE: One key expires, database dies: cache stampede
HOOK: Your cache hit rate is 99% and your database still went down — because the 1% arrived all at once, the moment one hot key expired.
ARC: 1) A hot key like the homepage feed expires; ten thousand in-flight requests miss simultaneously and all run the same expensive query — the herd kills the database, not the miss rate. 2) Three production fixes: request coalescing (Go's singleflight collapses duplicate calls), TTL jitter so keys never expire together, and serving stale data while one worker refreshes. 3) Facebook's 'Scaling Memcache' paper (NSDI 2013) formalized the same idea as leases — one client rebuilds, everyone else waits.
PAYOFF: Averages lie — systems fail on correlated behavior, and expiry timestamps are the easiest way to accidentally synchronize ten thousand clients.
QUESTION: Jittered TTLs or never-expire with background refresh — what does your team actually ship?
exemplars.long:
TITLE: The celebrity problem: timeline fanout at scale
HOOK: When a celebrity with 80 million followers tweets, a naive design performs 80 million writes for one 280-character message. Timeline architecture is deciding when that work is worth it.
ARC: 1) Fanout-on-read stores each tweet once and assembles timelines by querying every followee at read time — but Twitter reported timeline reads around 300,000 QPS against only thousands of new tweets per second, so reads melt first. 2) Fanout-on-write flips it: each tweet's ID is pushed into every follower's precomputed timeline, which Twitter kept in Redis — a read becomes one list fetch in milliseconds. 3) Then the celebrity problem: 80 million inserts for one tweet is a write storm that can lag by minutes. 4) The shipped answer is hybrid — fan out normal users on write, merge celebrity tweets in at read time, bounding work on both paths.
PAYOFF: There is no correct architecture, only a read/write ratio — precompute for the many, compute on demand for the heavy, and the cutoff is a dial, not a truth.
QUESTION: At what follower count would you flip a user from push to pull? Defend your number.

modules.label: CS Fundamentals
modules.style: the magic-removal channel: what REALLY happens beneath the software — bits, syscalls, packets, caches — so the viewer can re-explain it to a friend; one 'your computer is lying to you' reveal per video

submodules.label: How Computers Work
submodules.style: Silicon up to software: transistors, gates, binary, CPU cycles, the memory hierarchy — how code becomes electricity. OS abstractions start next door. Great episodes build one layer from the layer below it. Credibility: the latency ladder (L1 about 1ns, RAM about 100ns, SSD about 100µs), fetch-decode-execute, real instructions.

submodules.label: Operating Systems
submodules.style: The kernel's contract: processes versus threads, syscalls, scheduling, virtual memory, file descriptors. Hardware belongs to How Computers Work; packets to Networking. Great episodes catch the OS lying helpfully — virtual addresses, buffered writes. Credibility: strace output, fork and exec, page-fault mechanics, context-switch costs.

submodules.label: Networking & the Internet
submodules.style: Data in flight: IP, TCP and UDP, DNS, HTTP's evolution, TLS, routing — the full journey of a packet between machines. Inside-the-box concerns stay with Operating Systems. Great episodes trace one real request hop by hop. Credibility: handshake sequences, port numbers, dig/curl/traceroute output, RTT math.

submodules.label: Security & Cryptography Basics
submodules.style: How trust works: hashing versus encryption, symmetric and asymmetric keys, certificates, password storage, and the canonical attacks — SQL injection, XSS, MITM. Great episodes demo the attack, then the defense mechanism. Credibility: bcrypt-not-SHA-256 for passwords, TLS certificate chains, real breach post-mortems, OWASP names.

exemplars.short:
TITLE: 0.1 plus 0.2 isn't 0.3: floating point
HOOK: Open any browser console and type 0.1 + 0.2. The answer — 0.30000000000000004 — is not a bug, and it ships in every language you have ever used.
ARC: 1) Doubles are IEEE 754 binary64 — 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits, 52 fraction bits — so every number must be built from powers of two. 2) 0.1 in binary is 0.000110011... repeating forever, so the nearest 64-bit double is slightly off — add two rounding errors and they surface at the 17th digit. 3) That is why money code uses integer cents or decimal types: Python's decimal, Java's BigDecimal, Postgres NUMERIC.
PAYOFF: Floats aren't broken — they're honest about a hard truth: you cannot store infinite digits in 64 bits, so every float is the nearest representable lie.
QUESTION: Have you ever shipped a float-for-money bug — and how far into production did it get?
exemplars.long:
TITLE: Enter to pixels: what one URL triggers
HOOK: Pressing Enter on google.com fires four protocols across dozens of machines you will never see — and the whole negotiation usually finishes in a few hundred milliseconds.
ARC: 1) DNS first: browser and OS caches, then a recursive resolver walks root, .com TLD, and authoritative servers — classically over UDP port 53 — to return an IP. 2) TCP next: the three-way handshake — SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK — burns one full round-trip before a single byte of data moves. 3) TLS 1.3 needs just one more round-trip to agree on keys, down from two in TLS 1.2, after verifying the certificate chain up to a trusted root CA. 4) The HTTP request finally hits port 443, likely multiplexed over HTTP/2, and the HTML response starts parsing before it finishes downloading. 5) Since cross-continent round-trips run around 150-250ms, CDNs win by terminating your connection at an edge server a few milliseconds away.
PAYOFF: The internet gets faster not with faster light but with fewer round-trips — TLS 1.3, HTTP/2, and QUIC are all wars on RTT.
QUESTION: A site is slow: which layer do you blame first — DNS, TCP, TLS, or the app?

modules.label: Key Technologies
modules.style: one tool, deeply: why it exists, the mental model in one sentence, the handful of commands/APIs that cover 90% of real use, and the classic production mistake made with it

submodules.label: Git
submodules.style: Git's real model — objects, refs, the index — and the workflows above it: rebase versus merge, reflog rescue, bisect. Great episodes replace command memorization with the pointer picture. Credibility: .git internals via cat-file, exact recovery sequences, merge-conflict anatomy.

submodules.label: Nginx
submodules.style: Nginx as the front door: reverse proxying, server and location blocks, the worker event model, load balancing, TLS termination, caching directives. Great episodes read a real nginx.conf line by line. Credibility: proxy_pass semantics, location matching-order rules, worker_connections math, 502-versus-504 diagnosis.

submodules.label: Redis
submodules.style: Redis itself: data structures per use case, the single-threaded event loop, RDB versus AOF persistence, eviction policies, TTLs. Where caching sits in an architecture is System Design's lane. Great episodes match a structure to a job. Credibility: exact commands (ZADD, SETNX), maxmemory-policy options, O(1)-versus-O(n) command costs, port 6379.

submodules.label: GraphQL
submodules.style: GraphQL the contract: schemas, resolvers, queries versus mutations, the N+1 resolver trap, caching pain, and an honest comparison with REST. Great episodes weigh real costs, not advocacy. Credibility: actual SDL and resolver code, DataLoader batching, persisted queries, GitHub's public GraphQL API as the worked example.

submodules.label: WebSockets & gRPC
submodules.style: Beyond request-response: the WebSocket upgrade handshake and frames, gRPC over HTTP/2 with protobuf, streaming modes, and when plain HTTP still wins. Great episodes derive the protocol choice from the requirement. Credibility: the 101 Switching Protocols exchange, .proto definitions, gRPC's four streaming modes, the browser gRPC-Web caveat.

submodules.label: Kafka
submodules.style: Kafka's log-centric model: topics, partitions, offsets, consumer groups, retention, ordering guarantees. Generic queueing theory sits in System Design. Great episodes show why the log beats the queue for replay. Credibility: partition-count decisions, acks=all semantics, consumer-group rebalances, the 7-day default retention.

submodules.label: Auth & OAuth
submodules.style: who are you, prove it — sessions vs JWT, password hashing, OAuth2 flows with PKCE, OIDC, SSO/SAML, RBAC. Great episodes walk one real login flow arrow by arrow and flag the vulnerability each step prevents.

exemplars.short:
TITLE: git reset --hard isn't fatal: reflog rescue
HOOK: You just ran git reset --hard on the wrong branch and watched a day of work vanish. It's still there — Git almost never deletes a commit.
ARC: 1) Every time HEAD moves, Git appends a line to .git/logs/HEAD — run git reflog and your 'lost' commit is sitting right there as HEAD@{1}. 2) git reset --hard HEAD@{1}, or cherry-pick the raw hash, restores it — even unreachable commits survive until garbage collection, 30 days by default. 3) The same move rescues botched rebases and deleted branches — anything that was ever committed can come back.
PAYOFF: Git is an append-only object database with pointers on top — 'destructive' commands only move pointers, and the reflog remembers where they pointed.
QUESTION: Worst Git state you've ever recovered from — did you reflog your way out or quietly re-clone?
exemplars.long:
TITLE: Kafka's speed secret: it barely does anything
HOOK: Kafka pushes millions of messages a second on ordinary disks — not by avoiding the disk, but by using it the one way disks are actually fast.
ARC: 1) A topic splits into partitions, each an append-only log file; producers write sequentially, and sequential disk I/O runs orders of magnitude faster than random seeks. 2) The broker barely buffers in process — it leans on the OS page cache and ships bytes to consumers via sendfile() zero-copy, skipping user space entirely. 3) Consumers pull from offsets they control; a consumer group splits partitions among members — 12 partitions across 4 consumers is 3 each, and a 13th consumer sits idle. 4) Ordering holds per partition only: same key, same partition via hash — global order means one partition, which means no parallelism. 5) Retention is time- or size-based — 7 days by default, port 9092 — not consumption-based, so replaying last week is free.
PAYOFF: Kafka is fast because it's a dumb pipe on purpose — no per-message state, no delivery tracking; every consumer keeps its own bookmark.
QUESTION: How many partitions do you give a new topic — and what's your story when that number turns out wrong?

modules.label: AI & ML
modules.style: practitioner AI, zero hype: how it actually works (tokens, embeddings, attention in plain words), real API code with real costs, and the failure modes; never 'AI changes everything' filler

submodules.label: ML Fundamentals
submodules.style: Classical ML from scratch: regression, gradient descent, loss functions, overfitting, train/test discipline, evaluation metrics. LLM-specific topics stay in their lanes. Great episodes build tiny working models in NumPy or scikit-learn. Credibility: runnable code, the precision-recall trade-off, learning curves, why accuracy lies on imbalanced data.

submodules.label: LLMs & GenAI
submodules.style: What LLMs are: tokens, embeddings, attention in plain words, sampling, context windows, the model landscape. Prompting technique and app-building have their own lanes. Great episodes make the mechanism click without math worship. Credibility: real tokenizer output, temperature and top-p effects, context sizes and prices of named models.

submodules.label: Prompt Engineering
submodules.style: Getting reliably better outputs: few-shot examples, chain-of-thought, structured outputs, system prompts, prompt evaluation. Retrieval and tools belong to Agents & RAG. Great episodes show before-and-after outputs on the same task. Credibility: exact prompts on screen, JSON-mode and schema features, measured accuracy deltas, model-specific quirks.

submodules.label: Agents & RAG
submodules.style: Making models use knowledge and tools: embeddings, chunking, vector search, reranking, tool-calling loops, agent failure modes. Great episodes debug why retrieval returned the wrong paragraphs. Credibility: embedding model names with prices, recall@k evals, function-calling JSON, honest agent-reliability numbers.

submodules.label: Building AI Apps
submodules.style: Shipping AI features: API integration, streaming, cost and latency budgets, caching, evals, guardrails, fallbacks. How models work internally is upstream. Great episodes treat the model as an unreliable dependency and engineer around it. Credibility: real SDK code, per-token price math, p95 latencies, rate-limit strategies.

exemplars.short:
TITLE: Why LLMs can't count letters: tokens
HOOK: Frontier models have famously failed to count the r's in 'strawberry' — while writing working compilers. The letters were never there to count.
ARC: 1) Models don't read characters: a BPE tokenizer chops text into subword chunks first — GPT-4o's vocabulary is around 200,000 tokens — and 'strawberry' can arrive as pieces like 'str' + 'awberry', already as integer IDs. 2) Each ID becomes an embedding vector; nothing in that vector preserves spelling, so asking about letters asks for information the encoding destroyed. 3) Same root cause behind weak digit arithmetic and rhyming — and why 'spell it out letter by letter first' often fixes it.
PAYOFF: An LLM's dumbest failures usually trace to its input encoding — before blaming the model, ask what the tokenizer did to the text.
QUESTION: What's the most trivial thing you've watched a frontier model fail at — and can you pin it on tokenization?
exemplars.long:
TITLE: RAG that actually works: the retrieval pipeline
HOOK: Most 'chat with your docs' demos die in production for the same reason — the model never hallucinated; your retrieval handed it the wrong paragraphs.
ARC: 1) Ingest: split documents into chunks of a few hundred tokens with overlap — chunking strategy moves answer quality more than model choice does. 2) Embed each chunk — OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small costs $0.02 per million tokens — and store the vectors in pgvector or a dedicated vector database. 3) At query time, embed the question and take cosine-similarity top-k — but similar is not relevant: 'how do I cancel?' happily matches both the refund policy and the retention script. 4) The fixes that move the needle: hybrid search combining BM25 with vectors, a reranker model over the top 50 candidates, and metadata filters applied before similarity. 5) Ground the generation — pass chunks with citations, instruct 'answer only from context' — then evaluate retrieval hit-rate separately from answer quality.
PAYOFF: RAG quality is a search problem wearing an AI costume — measure recall@k on your retriever before touching prompts or swapping models.
QUESTION: Hybrid search plus a reranker, or a bigger context window stuffed with more chunks — where does your money go?

subjects.label: History
subjects.audience: students (school to UPSC aspirants) and history-curious viewers worldwide; Indian history in depth plus world history
subjects.style: story-driven; causes and consequences over rote dates; timelines and maps as diagrams; make it feel like a thriller, cite the numbers that stun

modules.label: Ancient India
modules.style: evidence-first storytelling: lead with what was actually found (seals, edicts, coins, ruins) and what it proves; explicitly separate archaeology from legend, and date everything

submodules.label: Indus Valley Civilisation
submodules.style: Cities before empires: planned streets, standardised bricks and seals, the undeciphered script, the still-open decline debate. Lead with excavated evidence from named sites (Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira) and always separate what digs prove from what we infer.

submodules.label: Vedic Age
submodules.style: The world the Vedas describe: pastoral clans becoming kingdoms, sabha and samiti, varna's beginnings, iron and the eastward push. Evidence is mostly textual — say so on screen — and keep date ranges hedged (around 1500-600 BCE).

submodules.label: Mahajanapadas, Buddhism & Jainism
submodules.style: second urbanisation to shramana revolution — Buddha and Mahavira as historical figures; councils, sects, texts and sites with exam-grade precision

submodules.label: Mauryan Empire
submodules.style: India's first empire, Chandragupta to Ashoka: Arthashastra statecraft, Megasthenes' account, rock and pillar edicts as primary sources. Anchor every claim in an edict, a Greek report or archaeology, with Kalinga as the hinge of the story.

submodules.label: Post-Mauryan India
submodules.style: the connector centuries — Kushanas, Satavahanas, Indo-Greeks; coins, art schools and Indo-Roman trade as historical evidence

submodules.label: Sangam Age & Early South India
submodules.style: Tamilakam's three crowns and Sangam literature — anthologies, Tirukkural, Muziris trade; the South enters Indian history

submodules.label: Gupta Empire
submodules.style: The 'classical age' and its fine print: Samudragupta's Prayag Prashasti, gold coinage, Aryabhata, Kalidasa, Nalanda. Cite the inscription or text behind each claim, and weigh the golden-age label against who it left out.

exemplars.short:
TITLE: The Great Bath: A 4,500-Year-Old Pool That Held Water
HOOK: Around 2500 BCE, workers in Mohenjo-daro waterproofed a public pool with natural tar. When archaeologists dug it up in the 1920s, the brickwork was still tight.
ARC: 1) The tank: around 12 by 7 metres, sunk into the citadel, with steps at both ends. 2) The engineering: baked bricks on edge in gypsum mortar with a bitumen layer — no cement, no pumps. 3) The meaning: no palace or grand temple found nearby; the city's biggest structure was civic.
PAYOFF: Harappans monumentalised the public bath, not the king — you can read a civilization's values in what it builds biggest.
QUESTION: What does India's biggest public structure today say about us?
exemplars.long:
TITLE: Ashoka's Regret: The Emperor Who Apologised in Stone
HOOK: Around 261 BCE, an emperor won a war so completely that he spent the rest of his life apologising for it — and carved the apology across the subcontinent.
ARC: 1) Kalinga: Rock Edict XIII, in Ashoka's own words, records around 100,000 killed and 150,000 deported. 2) The turn: dhamma — tolerance, hospitals, tree-lined roads — as state policy. 3) The machinery: edicts in Prakrit, written in Brahmi, placed on trade routes; dhamma-mahamattas as a new cadre of officials. 4) The export: his son Mahinda's mission takes Buddhism to Sri Lanka. 5) The rediscovery: Brahmi was forgotten until James Prinsep deciphered it in 1837 — India's greatest emperor was nearly erased.
PAYOFF: Almost everything we know of Ashoka comes from his own inscriptions — a ruler who published his remorse.
QUESTION: Is an apology carved in stone real accountability, or the world's oldest PR campaign?

modules.label: Medieval India
modules.style: power, money and armies: tell each reign through decisions and their costs — revenue systems, battles with real numbers, succession gambles; courts and cultures, not just kings

submodules.label: Harsha & Early Medieval North India
submodules.style: post-Gupta north India — Harsha, the tripartite Kannauj struggle, Rajput origins, the Palas; lean on sources like Hiuen Tsang and prashastis

submodules.label: Cholas, Pallavas & the Deccan Dynasties
submodules.style: the imperial South — temple-building states, Rajendra's naval expeditions, Uttaramerur village democracy; inscriptions as evidence

submodules.label: Delhi Sultanate
submodules.style: Five dynasties in 320 years: how Turkic cavalry states ruled from Delhi — iqta revenue, Alauddin's market control, Tughlaq's experiments, Timur's 1398 sack. Focus on power mechanics and administration over battle lists; reign dates exact.

submodules.label: Bhakti & Sufi Movements
submodules.style: saints who reshaped India — saguna/nirguna, Alvars to Kabir to Nanak, Chishti orders; composite culture with dates and places

submodules.label: Regional Kingdoms of Medieval India
submodules.style: India between Sultanate and Mughals — Bahmani, Bengal, Mewar, the Ahoms; the 1500 map nobody teaches

submodules.label: Vijayanagara Empire
submodules.style: The empire travellers raved about: Hampi's bazaars and temples, Krishnadevaraya's court, Talikota 1565. Pair every splendour claim with its eyewitness — Abdur Razzaq, Domingo Paes, Nicolo Conti — and read the ruins as evidence.

submodules.label: Mughal Empire
submodules.style: Empire as a system: mansabdari ranks, jagir transfers, Akbar's sulh-i-kul, Todar Mal's revenue settlement, Aurangzeb's long Deccan drain. Explain how the machine worked and why it seized up, with reign dates and named institutions.

submodules.label: Marathas
submodules.style: From Shivaji's forts to a confederacy taxing half of India: guerrilla war, the Ashtapradhan, the Peshwa shift, chauth and sardeshmukhi, Panipat 1761. Explain the revenue-and-cavalry model that scaled a mountain kingdom into a subcontinental power.

exemplars.short:
TITLE: Token Money, 1329: Delhi's Boldest Economic Disaster
HOOK: In 1329, Delhi's Sultan declared that cheap brass tokens were worth as much as silver coins. His subjects heard: print your own money at home.
ARC: 1) The idea: Muhammad bin Tughlaq faced a silver shortage and copied China's paper-money logic with token currency. 2) The flaw: no defence against forgery — the chronicler Barani wrote that every house became a mint. 3) The retreat: the Sultan redeemed the fakes with real silver, draining his own treasury.
PAYOFF: Money is a trust technology — Tughlaq had the fiat idea 600 years early, without the state capacity to enforce it.
QUESTION: Was Tughlaq a fool or just early? Your UPI balance runs on the same trust.
exemplars.long:
TITLE: Panipat 1526: How 12,000 Beat 100,000
HOOK: On 21 April 1526, a Kabul prince with around 12,000 men faced the Delhi Sultan's army of around 100,000 with war elephants. By afternoon the Sultan was dead.
ARC: 1) The stakes: Babur, descendant of Timur, on his fifth push into Hindustan; Ibrahim Lodi's nobles already defecting. 2) The tech: matchlock muskets and field cannon behind a chained line of around 700 carts — the araba. 3) The trap: tulughma flanking — horse archers wheel around both wings and shoot into the packed centre. 4) The collapse: Lodi's mass is pressed onto the gun line; Ibrahim dies on the field, the only Delhi Sultan to fall in battle. 5) The aftermath: Delhi and Agra taken; Babur records it all in the Baburnama.
PAYOFF: Numbers lose to combined arms — and the victor who writes a memoir wins twice.
QUESTION: Without the cannons, does Babur still win — or did Lodi's fractured nobility matter more?

modules.label: Modern India
modules.style: the freedom struggle and after with exact dates, acts and people; every episode connects the event to something visible in today's India (a law, a border, an institution)

submodules.label: Eighteenth-Century India
submodules.style: Mughal collapse to Company rise — successor states, Mysore, the Sikhs; end on the 'dark age or decentralisation' debate

submodules.label: British Raj
submodules.style: How a trading company became a state and then a Crown colony: Plassey to 1947 through revenue systems, railways, famines and the drain theory. Name the Acts and the numbers; show both what was built and who paid for it.

submodules.label: Freedom Struggle
submodules.style: The campaigns that ended an empire: 1857, Swadeshi, Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Quit India, the INA. Dates, places and people exact; show strategy, internal debates and costs — not just heroism.

submodules.label: Post-Independence India
submodules.style: The republic under construction: princely integration, the 1950 Constitution, linguistic states, wars, the Green Revolution, Emergency, 1991 reforms. Every episode ties one decision to a consequence Indians live with today.

exemplars.short:
TITLE: The Radcliffe Line: Drawn in Five Weeks
HOOK: The border that defines South Asia was drawn by a British lawyer who had never been to India before — in around five weeks.
ARC: 1) July 1947: Cyril Radcliffe chairs two boundary commissions armed with outdated maps and census tables. 2) The line splits Punjab and Bengal through villages, canals and families — and is kept secret until 17 August, two days AFTER independence. 3) Around 14 million people cross it; estimates of the dead run from several hundred thousand to around 2 million.
PAYOFF: Radcliffe refused his fee and never returned to India.
QUESTION: Announcing the line before independence — fewer deaths, or more? Argue it.
exemplars.long:
TITLE: 562 Kingdoms Gone: How India's Map Was Made
HOOK: On 15 August 1947, India as one country did not exist — over 560 princely states covering around a third of the land could legally have stayed out.
ARC: 1) The problem: British paramountcy lapsed, and each ruler chose India, Pakistan, or going it alone. 2) The team: Sardar Patel and V.P. Menon with the Instrument of Accession — just defence, foreign affairs and communications. 3) The persuasion: privy purses and guarantees; nearly all sign before independence day. 4) The holdouts: Junagadh's plebiscite, Hyderabad's Operation Polo in September 1948, Kashmir's October accession amid invasion. 5) The finish: mergers, then the 1956 linguistic reorganisation dissolves the princely map entirely.
PAYOFF: Modern India was assembled mostly by paperwork and pressure — force was the exception, not the method.
QUESTION: Patel is called India's Bismarck. Fair, or does negotiation beat blood-and-iron?

modules.label: Ancient World
modules.style: make dead civilizations feel present: daily life, engineering feats and stunning scale numbers; always one comparison to something Indian or modern so scale lands

submodules.label: Ancient Egypt
submodules.style: The Nile's civilization through its evidence: how pyramids were actually built (paid workers' villages), mummification's logic, Karnak, the Rosetta decipherment. Kill the slave-labour and alien myths with excavation reports and named finds.

submodules.label: Greece & Rome
submodules.style: Institutions and engineering with dates: Athens' assembly, Sparta's system, Alexander's decade of conquest, Rome's republic-to-empire slide, concrete, roads and aqueducts. Named figures and primary sources over vague 'glory of the ancients'.

submodules.label: Mesopotamia & Persia
submodules.style: Firsts of civilization and the tablets that prove them: cuneiform receipts, Hammurabi's 282 laws, ziggurats, then Persia's Royal Road and satrap system under Cyrus and Darius. Lead with the invention or institution, not the king list.

submodules.label: Ancient China
submodules.style: Dynasties as systems: Qin standardisation and the terracotta army, Han bureaucracy and the exam idea, Silk Road exchange, the paper-to-gunpowder inventions. Connect each dynasty to the institution or invention it left behind.

exemplars.short:
TITLE: Pyramid Builders: Paid Workers, Not Slaves
HOOK: The people who built the Great Pyramid ate beef, drank beer rations, and got medical care. We found their town.
ARC: 1) The evidence: the workers' village at Giza, excavated since the 1990s — bakeries, breweries, cattle bones by the thousand. 2) The organisation: rotating labour gangs who scrawled names like 'Friends of Khufu' inside the pyramid's relieving chambers. 3) The scale: around 2.3 million blocks in roughly 20 years — a block placed every few minutes of daylight.
PAYOFF: The pyramid was a state logistics project — the real wonder is the payroll.
QUESTION: Which is harder to believe: aliens, or a 4,500-year-old supply chain that worked?
exemplars.long:
TITLE: Feeding Rome: A Million Mouths, Zero Tractors
HOOK: Ancient Rome grew to around a million people — a size London only reached in the 1800s. Every day, all of them had to be fed by sail and muscle.
ARC: 1) The dole: the annona gave free or subsidised grain to around 200,000 registered citizens. 2) The sources: Egypt and North Africa as grain provinces — a delayed fleet meant riots in the capital. 3) The ports: Ostia and the artificial harbour at Portus; barges hauled up the Tiber by oxen. 4) The politics: 'bread and circuses' is Juvenal's sneer — emperors rose and fell on the grain supply. 5) The end: when the provinces fractured in the 5th century, the city starved and shrank to tens of thousands.
PAYOFF: Rome didn't fall in a single battle; its supply chain did.
QUESTION: Which single supply line could break a megacity today?

modules.label: World History
modules.style: turning points told through people under pressure: the decision, the stakes, the aftermath; real casualty and economic figures, and more than one side's perspective

submodules.label: Empires & Dynasties
submodules.style: Rise-and-fall mechanics beyond Europe: the Mongol relay post and composite bow, Ottoman devshirme, Mali's gold and Mansa Musa's hajj, Habsburg marriages. Name the system that scaled each empire and the flaw that broke it.

submodules.label: Renaissance & Enlightenment
submodules.style: Europe rewires its mind — Florence to Luther to Voltaire; the ideas that armed the revolutions

submodules.label: Revolutions
submodules.style: Why regimes snap: French, American, Russian, Chinese — the fiscal crisis, the spark, the radical turn, the aftermath that betrays the slogans. Compare across cases with exact dates and named actors.

submodules.label: The Industrial Revolution
submodules.style: coal, cotton, railways — why Britain first, how it spread, what it did to workers; numbers over adjectives

submodules.label: The Age of Isms
submodules.style: the age of isms — capitalism to communism to fascism; the unifications of Italy and Germany as ideology in action

submodules.label: Colonization & Decolonization
submodules.style: empire built and dismantled — 1492 to 1994; Berlin Conference, Sykes-Picot, Bandung; maps redrawn, with dates

submodules.label: World Wars
submodules.style: Two wars as decisions under pressure: the July 1914 spiral, trench mechanics, Versailles' backlash, appeasement, D-Day, the bomb. Real orders and hedged casualty figures, always with more than one nation's perspective.

submodules.label: Cold War
submodules.style: A 45-year standoff through its flashpoints: Berlin airlift, Cuba 1962, proxy wars, the space race, 1989. Decisions and near-misses with declassified detail (Arkhipov, Able Archer 83) over ideology lectures.

exemplars.short:
TITLE: The Wrong Turn That Started World War One
HOOK: On 28 June 1914, a driver in Sarajevo took a wrong turn and stalled the car — directly in front of a 19-year-old assassin who had already given up.
ARC: 1) That morning a grenade had missed Archduke Franz Ferdinand; the route was changed, but nobody told the drivers. 2) The stall: the car stops beside Gavrilo Princip outside a delicatessen; two shots. 3) The spiral: Austria's ultimatum, Russia mobilises, Germany's war plan demands speed — five weeks later, Europe is at war.
PAYOFF: The system was primed to explode; mobilisation timetables made de-escalation nearly impossible. The wrong turn just struck the match.
QUESTION: No wrong turn — no World War One, or just a different spark within months?
exemplars.long:
TITLE: One Vote From Nuclear War: October 1962
HOOK: On 27 October 1962, three Soviet officers in a suffocating submarine voted on whether to fire a nuclear torpedo. The vote was two to one.
ARC: 1) Day twelve of the Cuban Missile Crisis: a US blockade, and a U-2 shot down that very day. 2) Submarine B-59: days out of radio contact, batteries dying, air near 45°C, US ships dropping practice depth charges to force it up. 3) The rule: launch needed all three senior officers — the captain and political officer said yes; Vasili Arkhipov said no. 4) The exit: the sub surfaces; within days Kennedy and Khrushchev cut the secret Jupiter-missiles-for-Cuba deal. 5) The silence: the story stayed buried until around 2002.
PAYOFF: Deterrence theory didn't save the world that day — one calm officer did.
QUESTION: Should any single person hold veto power over nuclear use? Design your answer.

modules.label: History of Everyday Things
modules.style: the secret biography of everyday objects: the accident, the inventor, the trade route; every episode ends at the viewer's own table — 'that's why yours looks like this'

submodules.label: Inventions & Discoveries
submodules.style: The accident-and-iteration truth behind things we use: penicillin's contaminated dish, the microwave's melted chocolate bar, GPS born from tracking Sputnik. Real inventor names and dates — and the decades between discovery and product.

submodules.label: Food & Drink
submodules.style: How dishes and drinks moved history: spice routes, the Columbian exchange (chilli reached India with the Portuguese), tea and opium, coffee houses. Trace one item's journey with dates and trade numbers; flag food-origin myths honestly.

submodules.label: Money & Trade
submodules.style: From cowrie shells to UPI: Lydian coins around 600 BCE, Song paper money, bills of exchange, the gold standard's 1971 end, why trade routes shifted. Every episode shows who trusted whom, and what enforced that trust.

submodules.label: Medicine & Disease
submodules.style: Plagues and cures that reshaped societies: the Black Death's labour shock, Jenner and vaccination in 1796, cholera and the Broad Street pump, antibiotics and resistance. Body counts hedged; the mechanism-and-response story exact.

exemplars.short:
TITLE: Coca-Cola's Secret: It Really Had Cocaine
HOOK: For its first two decades, Coca-Cola's name was literal — coca leaf extract in every glass.
ARC: 1) 1886: Atlanta pharmacist John Pemberton sells it as a nerve tonic — 'coca' for the leaf, 'kola' for the caffeine nut. 2) Around 1903, drug panic pushes the company to switch to 'spent', decocainised leaves — flavour stays, drug goes. 3) The company still imports coca leaves today under a special licence, processed by one authorised firm.
PAYOFF: Brands outlive their products — the name is a fossil of a Victorian pharmacy counter.
QUESTION: Which everyday product today will look shocking in a hundred years?
exemplars.long:
TITLE: From Shells to UPI: Money's 3,000-Year Trust Trick
HOOK: A cowrie shell, a lump of electrum, a paper note, a QR code — none of them are worth anything by themselves. That is exactly the point.
ARC: 1) Commodity money: cowries circulate across Africa and Asia — scarce, portable, uncounterfeitable. 2) Around 600 BCE, Lydia mints the first standardised coins; the king's stamp replaces weighing at every sale. 3) Song China issues jiaozi, the first widespread paper money, around 1000 CE — and promptly discovers inflation by over-printing. 4) Goldsmiths' receipts become banknotes; in 1971 Nixon ends dollar-gold convertibility — money becomes pure fiat. 5) UPI processes over 15 billion transactions a month — trust has moved from metal to state to protocol.
PAYOFF: Every era's money is a claim on trust; the technology changes, the trick never does.
QUESTION: Is crypto the next link in this chain — or a repeat of Tughlaq's token money?

subjects.label: Geography
subjects.audience: students and exam aspirants (school, SSC, UPSC) plus map-curious viewers worldwide
subjects.style: map-first thinking; explain WHY places are the way they are; use diagrams for physical processes and charts for rankings

modules.label: India — Physical
modules.style: India's landscape as a story of forces: why the mountain, river or monsoon is exactly where it is — real heights, lengths and rainfall figures; UPSC-grade names told creator-grade

submodules.label: Mountains & Plateaus
submodules.style: Why the relief exists: the Himalayan collision, the Deccan Trap's stacked lava flows, the Aravallis' age. Real heights and ages, and what each landform does to the climate, rivers and people around it.

submodules.label: Indian Physiography
submodules.style: India's divisions beyond the mountains — plains, coasts, islands, lakes; bhabar/terai/khadar/bangar-level precision

submodules.label: Rivers
submodules.style: One river system at a time: source, tributaries, gradient, and what each stretch enables — dams, disputes, deltas. Exact lengths and basin figures hedged where sources differ, and always the why behind the river's behaviour.

submodules.label: Monsoon & Climate
submodules.style: The monsoon as a machine: differential heating, the ITCZ shift, Arabian Sea vs Bay of Bengal branches, El Niño's interference, bursts and breaks. Real rainfall figures and named places; mechanism before memorisation.

submodules.label: Soils & Vegetation
submodules.style: ICAR's eight soils and India's forest types — the classic prelims area taught as soil-crop-region triads

exemplars.short:
TITLE: Mawsynram: 11,000 mm of Rain a Year
HOOK: One village in Meghalaya gets around 11,000 millimetres of rain a year — Mumbai's annual downpour, five times over.
ARC: 1) The funnel: Bay of Bengal monsoon winds get squeezed into converging Khasi hill valleys. 2) The wall: air forced up around 1,400 metres cools and dumps — orographic rain, nearly all of it between June and September. 3) The twist: villagers still face water shortage in winter — the deluge runs straight off the slopes.
PAYOFF: 'Wettest place on Earth' and 'water-scarce' can be the same village — rainfall is not water security.
QUESTION: Name another place where abundance and scarcity coexist like this.
exemplars.long:
TITLE: The Himalayas Are Still Growing
HOOK: The mountain range on your map is a live collision — India is still ramming into Asia at about the speed your fingernails grow.
ARC: 1) The journey: the Indian plate broke off Gondwana and raced north, colliding around 50 million years ago. 2) The proof: marine fossils sit in the limestone near Everest's summit — that rock was once sea floor. 3) The rate: convergence of around 4-5 cm a year; Everest rises around 4 mm a year even as erosion files it down. 4) The receipts: the 2015 Nepal earthquake — strain releasing in jolts along the Main Himalayan Thrust. 5) The elders: the Indus and Sutlej are older than the range — antecedent rivers that kept cutting as the mountains rose around them.
PAYOFF: The Himalaya is a process, not a place — and its earthquakes are the instalment payments.
QUESTION: Should Himalayan towns build to Japanese seismic codes? Who pays for that?

modules.label: India — Economic
modules.style: geography that pays: why crops, industries and ports sit where they sit — resource logic, transport logic, one named company, crop belt or port as the running example

submodules.label: Agriculture
submodules.style: Why crops grow where they do: soil types, rainfall lines, irrigation, and the pull of MSP and mandis. One crop belt per episode with hedged yield and state-share figures, and the economics that lock farmers in.

submodules.label: Minerals & Industry
submodules.style: The resource map's logic: why coal sits in the Damodar valley, iron ore in Odisha, and industry clusters at ports and coalfields. Named mines, plants and corridors, with production shares hedged.

submodules.label: Transport & Trade
submodules.style: How goods and people actually move: highways, rail freight corridors, ports, inland waterways. Real route names, tonnage and travel-time numbers, and why each corridor was placed where it is.

exemplars.short:
TITLE: Why Assam Grows Half of India's Tea
HOOK: Around half the tea India drinks comes from one river valley. That is not tradition — it is rainfall arithmetic.
ARC: 1) The recipe: tea wants heavy rain spread through the year, acidic loamy soil, and slopes that drain — the Brahmaputra valley delivers all three. 2) The history: the British found indigenous tea plants in Assam in the 1820s and built estates to break China's monopoly. 3) The scale: Assam produces around 700 million kg a year — more than most tea-growing countries manage.
PAYOFF: Crops don't follow culture or borders; they follow soil chemistry and rainfall lines.
QUESTION: If climate change shifts the rainfall belt, where does India's tea move next?
exemplars.long:
TITLE: The Golden Quadrilateral: 5,846 km That Rewired India
HOOK: In 2001, India began linking Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata with one highway loop. It quietly rearranged where Indians build, work and sell.
ARC: 1) The build: around 5,846 km under the National Highways Development Project — India's biggest transport build since the railways. 2) The physics: freight travel times on upgraded corridors fall by roughly a quarter, and reliability matters as much as speed. 3) The relocation: studies find manufacturing drifting out of big cities into towns close to the corridor. 4) The gap: districts far from the loop grew slower — a highway re-prices land unevenly. 5) The sequel: dedicated freight corridors and expressways now chase the same logic at higher speed.
PAYOFF: A road doesn't just carry traffic — it re-prices land and labour along its whole length.
QUESTION: Does connecting four metros help the towns between them, or drain them?

modules.label: World Geography
modules.style: the planet's greatest hits with the WHY behind each: real scale numbers, always compared back to India so the size actually registers

submodules.label: Continents & Oceans
submodules.style: The planet's biggest features and their why: drift's evidence, ocean currents as conveyor belts, why coastlines match across the Atlantic. Scale numbers always compared to something Indian so size actually registers.

submodules.label: Climate Zones
submodules.style: Why climate wraps the Earth in bands: Hadley cells, deserts near 30 degrees, equatorial rainforest, Mediterranean winters. Teach each zone through one named place living with its consequences.

submodules.label: Natural Wonders
submodules.style: One wonder per episode with the process that built it: the Grand Canyon's incision, the Great Barrier Reef's polyps, Victoria Falls' basalt cracks. Real dimensions and hedged ages, formation mechanism front and centre.

exemplars.short:
TITLE: The Pacific Ocean Is Shrinking
HOOK: The biggest thing on Earth is disappearing a few centimetres a year — and the Atlantic is eating its lunch.
ARC: 1) The mechanism: the Atlantic widens at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge by around 2-4 cm a year, while Pacific floor dives into subduction trenches. 2) The evidence: GPS stations measure the drift directly; the Ring of Fire is the Pacific's shrinking seam. 3) The forecast: over a couple of hundred million years, the Americas and Asia converge — the supercontinent cycle turns again.
PAYOFF: Oceans are temporary — the world map is one frame of a very slow film.
QUESTION: Which of today's countries end up neighbours on the next supercontinent?
exemplars.long:
TITLE: The Green Sahara: When the Desert Had Lakes
HOOK: Under the world's largest hot desert lie fish bones, hippo skeletons, and cave paintings of people swimming.
ARC: 1) The evidence: rock art at Tassili n'Ajjer shows swimmers and cattle herds; sediments record Lake Mega-Chad at around the size of a sea. 2) The mechanism: Earth's orbital wobble — precession on a roughly 23,000-year cycle — pulled the monsoon north during the African Humid Period, until around 5,000 years ago. 3) The flip: vegetation feedbacks made the drying fast once it started. 4) The exodus: herders retreated to the Nile valley — concentration that fed the rise of Egypt. 5) The kicker: the cycle continues; the Sahara is due to green again in the far future.
PAYOFF: Climate rebuilt and emptied whole worlds before humans burned anything — what's new today is the speed.
QUESTION: Did the drying Sahara create ancient Egypt? Argue both sides.

modules.label: Earth in Action
modules.style: forces in action: the mechanism step by step (plates, storms, ice, sand), then a named real event with its date and magnitude as proof

submodules.label: Plate Tectonics
submodules.style: The engine under the map: ridges, subduction, hotspots, and what happens at each boundary type. Real plate speeds in cm per year and named boundaries, with India's northward journey as the recurring case study.

submodules.label: Geomorphic Processes
submodules.style: the earth's sculptors — weathering to karst to coasts; every day a landform → process → real example ladder

submodules.label: Volcanoes & Earthquakes
submodules.style: Named events as evidence: why quakes cluster where they do, magnitude scales that multiply rather than add, volcano types by magma chemistry. Anchor each episode on one real event with date, magnitude and consequence.

submodules.label: Atmosphere & Winds
submodules.style: the air machine — heat budget, pressure belts, jet streams, local winds; every named wind located on the map

submodules.label: Weather & Storms
submodules.style: Storms from their ingredients: cyclones need around 26.5°C seas, tornado alley is an air-mass collision zone, lightning is charge separation. One named storm per episode with real wind speeds and pressure drops.

submodules.label: Oceanography
submodules.style: the ocean as a system — currents, tides, IOD, UNCLOS; fishing grounds and deep-sea resources argued with map logic

submodules.label: Glaciers & Deserts
submodules.style: Ice and sand as sculptors: U-valleys and moraines, dune types and their movement, why deserts sit where they sit. Hedged retreat rates and dune speeds, with named glaciers and deserts, never generic 'climate is changing' lines.

exemplars.short:
TITLE: Parícutin: The Volcano Born in a Cornfield
HOOK: In February 1943, a Mexican farmer watched a crack in his cornfield hiss, smoke, and start throwing rocks. Within a year it was a mountain over 300 metres tall.
ARC: 1) The birth: villagers watched the cinder cone grow house-high within days — the only volcano scientists observed from birth to extinction, 1943 to 1952. 2) The mechanism: gas-charged basaltic magma found a fresh vent; cinder cones grow fast and die young. 3) The trace: lava buried two villages — the San Juan church tower still pokes out of the flow.
PAYOFF: Mountains aren't scenery — some of them are events.
QUESTION: Would you rebuild beside a 'dead' volcano? How dead is dead?
exemplars.long:
TITLE: The 2004 Tsunami: One Quake, Fourteen Countries
HOOK: On 26 December 2004, the Indian Ocean floor slipped — and hours later the same wave was killing people on two continents.
ARC: 1) The source: a magnitude-around-9.1 megathrust off Sumatra; the fault unzipped for around 1,300 km. 2) The physics: in deep water a tsunami races at around 800 km/h with barely a ripple on the surface; near shore it slows and stacks into walls. 3) The toll: around 228,000 dead across 14 countries, from Indonesia to India to Somalia. 4) The failure: the Indian Ocean had no warning network — the Pacific had one for decades. 5) The fix: the Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System went live within about two years; buoys, sirens and drills now stand between the fault and the coast.
PAYOFF: The earthquake was unpreventable; most of the deaths were an information failure.
QUESTION: The warning tech now exists — so why do disaster deaths still track poverty lines?

modules.label: Human Geography
modules.style: people patterns: why cities boom, borders bend and millions migrate; real population numbers and one map oddity or paradox per episode

submodules.label: Cities & Megacities
submodules.style: Why cities sit where they sit and grow how they grow: site vs situation, primacy, informal settlements' internal logic. Hedged UN population figures and one named city's mechanics per episode, never a generic 'cities are growing' take.

submodules.label: Population & Migration
submodules.style: People flows with numbers: demographic transition stages, remittance corridors (India receives over $100 billion a year, hedged), Partition and other great migrations. Push-pull mechanics through one named flow per episode.

submodules.label: Borders & Strange Maps
submodules.style: The strangest lines on Earth and their paper trails: the India-Bangladesh enclave swap of 2015, the Durand and Radcliffe lines, why Mercator distorts. Every oddity explained by the treaty, survey or projection that created it.

exemplars.short:
TITLE: Tokyo: A City Bigger Than Australia
HOOK: More people live in and around Tokyo than in all of Australia — around 37 million against around 26 million.
ARC: 1) The shape: not one city but a merged galaxy of cities around Tokyo Bay — the world's largest urban area. 2) The enabler: the planet's densest rail network moves tens of millions of trips a day; density only works when people can move. 3) The paradox: Tokyo keeps growing while Japan's population shrinks — the capital is absorbing its own country.
PAYOFF: Megacities aren't crowded versions of cities — they're transport networks wearing buildings.
QUESTION: Is one giant capital a strength or a national risk? Think Tokyo, Seoul, Delhi.
exemplars.long:
TITLE: Megacity Century: From 10 to 34 in 30 Years
HOOK: In 1990 the planet had around ten cities of over ten million people. Today it has around 34 — and nearly all the new ones are in Asia and Africa.
ARC: 1) The list: Tokyo, Delhi, Shanghai, Dhaka, Lagos — a megacity is around ten million plus, and Delhi is projected among the largest of all. 2) The engine: rural push and urban pull — Dhaka adds several hundred thousand people a year. 3) The speed: Shenzhen went from a town of tens of thousands to over 12 million in around four decades — growth London needed 150 years for. 4) The form: much of it is informal — around a billion people worldwide live in slums (UN-Habitat figures). 5) The stakes: transport, water and sewage decide whether density becomes a superpower or a trap.
PAYOFF: Urbanisation on this scale happens roughly once per civilization — and Asia and Africa are mid-leap right now.
QUESTION: Should governments fight megacity growth or build for it? Pick a side with one example.

subjects.label: Math & Aptitude
subjects.audience: students and job-exam aspirants (SSC, Banking, CAT, placement tests) plus anyone who enjoys number tricks
subjects.style: trick-first: show the slow way, then the fast way; every video ends with one practice problem; use worked examples as text blocks

subjects.label: Science
subjects.audience: students and curious viewers of all ages worldwide, English
subjects.style: everyday-phenomena first (why does X happen?), then the principle; diagrams for mechanisms; one wow-fact per video

subjects.label: Money & Finance
subjects.audience: young earners and students learning to manage money; Indian instruments (₹, SIP, PPF, UPI) with globally useful concepts
subjects.style: numbers made visceral with real rupee examples; no stock tips, only concepts; always show the compounding math

subjects.label: English & Communication
subjects.audience: learners improving English for exams, interviews and confidence — India-first, useful worldwide
subjects.style: one rule or pattern per video with 3 real usage examples; common Indian-English mistakes handled kindly

modules.label: Grammar
modules.style: rules people actually break: state the rule ONCE in plain words, then spend the video on edge cases and the specific mistakes Indian speakers make — warmly, never like a textbook

submodules.label: Tenses
submodules.style: Owns time and aspect only — present perfect vs past, stative verbs, the since/for traps — not word-choice slips or article rules. Great episodes fix ONE contrast with verbatim pairs: 'I have been working here since 2019', never 'I am working here since 2019'.

submodules.label: Common Errors
submodules.style: The Indian-English slip clinic: 'discuss about', 'revert back', 'myself Anita', 'prepone', subject-verb misses — anything that isn't a tense or preposition rule. Explain WHY each slip feels right, give the verbatim fix, and say honestly when the 'error' is fine in India.
